name: Sagrada Família
label: Sagrada Família

text.description:
The Sagrada Família is the great basilica designed by Antoni Gaudí in Barcelona's Eixample district. Building began in 1882, and Gaudí took over the design the following year and gave it his own mix of Gothic and flowing Art Nouveau forms. He worked on it for the rest of his life and is buried in the crypt. When he died in 1926 it was far from finished, and work has carried on ever since. The central Tower of Jesus Christ is 172.5 m high, which makes this the tallest church in the world. Parts of the building, including the Nativity façade and the Crypt, are part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing for Gaudí's works.

It photographs well because nothing else looks like it. Dozens of carved spires, textured stonework and sculpted detail give your phone plenty to work with, even in a quick snap. The sheer height is the main challenge, so decide early whether you want the whole building or just a detail. From the phone icon on the map you are very close, so the towers will lean inwards if you tilt the phone upwards. That can look dramatic, but if you want straighter lines, step back and keep the phone level. Expect other visitors in the frame, so be patient and shoot in the gaps.
text.geographic_location: The Sagrada Família stands in the Eixample district of Barcelona. Sagrada Família Metro station is right beside it.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line L5 or Metro line L2 to Sagrada Família Metro station, which is about 1 minute on foot from the basilica, with the basilica to the south of the station. If you are coming by tram, tram T4 stops at Sicília, about 6 minutes on foot from the basilica, which lies to the north of the stop. Tram T4 also stops at Monumental Metro station (also on Metro line L2), about 9 minutes on foot from the basilica, which lies to the north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the towers into the frame from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the façade. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out spires and carved details high above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. If you want the whole building in one shot, walk a little further back from this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the vertical lines of the towers straight. Hold the phone as level as you can rather than tilting it far upwards. Look for a foreground element, such as people or a tree, to give the huge building some scale. For a close-up, fill the frame with the stone carving rather than trying to include everything.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the detail. If you want the full height in one frame, try panorama mode held vertically, moving slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shots. Around midday the sun is high and the light can be harsh on the stone.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the surrounding streets.

name: Park Güell
label: Park Güell

text.description: Park Güell is a hillside garden complex designed by Antoni Gaudí for the industrialist Eusebi Güell. It sits on the southern slope of the Turó del Carmel, so the city spreads out below it. It was meant to be a private estate of sixty villa plots, but only two houses were built. It opened to the public as a park in 1926 and is now a municipal garden. It is also part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing for Gaudí's works. It photographs well because almost everything is curved or colourful: the two gatehouses at the entrance, the long wavy bench around the main terrace, and the mosaic-covered vaulted space beneath it. The raised stone walkways have columns that look like tree trunks, which makes good leading lines. For the widest view, climb to the hill of the three crosses at the top, where the Sagrada Família, Torre Glòries, Montjuïc and the sea can be seen. Expect other visitors in most shots, so shoot a little higher or tighter to keep people out of the frame, or let them add a sense of scale. Keep your phone's lens clean, as you will be handling it a lot on the stairs and terraces. The main area has a ticket system and tickets often sell out, so book ahead where you can.
text.geographic_location: Park Güell is in the La Salut neighbourhood of Barcelona's Gràcia district, on the southern slope of the Turó del Carmel hill, at about 41.4136° N, 2.1528° E. It is a large site, around 854 m across, and it looks over the city from above the streets of Gràcia.
text.directions_text: The nearest stations are on Metro line L3. Vallcarca Metro station is about 716 m from the park, which is about 12 minutes on foot, and the park lies to the east of it. Lesseps Metro station is about 886 m away, which is about 14 minutes on foot, and the park lies to the north of it. The park sits on a hillside, so allow a little extra time. Once there, follow the park paths to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the terrace, the bench and the gatehouses. Use the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views of the walkways and columns. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for mosaic details and for distant views of the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Take a few steps either way along the path to get a clean line of sight without other visitors in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the curve of the bench or a walkway as a line leading into the frame. Include a bit of sky and city beyond the terrace edge to show the hillside setting. Keep the phone level so the architecture does not look tilted.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mosaics to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright tiles and sky do not wash out. If the sun is behind you, check the screen for your own shadow before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday is often harsh and busy.

label: Cathedral
camera_source: Commons cluster (158 photos). Moved 50 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 100 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description: Barcelona Cathedral, properly the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and Saint Eulalia, is the seat of the archbishop of Barcelona and the centrepiece of the old Gothic Quarter. The present building was begun on 1 May 1298 and took about 150 years, with the cloister finished in 1448. The tall neo-Gothic façade that many visitors picture was added later and completed in 1913, so the front looks younger than the sides. It photographs well because the towers, pointed pinnacles and carved gargoyles give you plenty of detail, and the stone looks different in every kind of light. The sources give the bell towers as 54 metres high, with the tallest point, the central lantern tower (cimborio), reaching 70 metres. Inside the cloister, 13 white geese are kept, one for each year of Saint Eulalia's life according to tradition. That is a charming small subject if you go in. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m east of the subject. From here you see the eastern end of the building rather than the façade. The streets around are narrow, so you will probably be tilting your phone upwards, and the cathedral will not fit in one shot unless you step back. Take a wide view first, then move to closer shots of the stonework and sculpture. Expect other visitors to wander through your frame, so be patient and take a few shots. Right next to it: Gothic Quarter and the Bishop's Bridge.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the Gothic Quarter (Barri Gòtic) in Barcelona's old town, a short walk from Jaume I Metro station.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line L4 to Jaume I Metro station, which is 194 m from the cathedral, about 3 minutes on foot, and walk west towards it. Liceu Metro station (Metro line L3) is also nearby: the cathedral is 392 m to the north-east of it, about 6 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are squeezed into a narrow street and cannot fit the towers in. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gargoyles, pinnacles and stone carving higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. If the view is blocked by people, move a few steps sideways rather than closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the towers upright against the vertical lines. Leave a little sky above the highest point so the central lantern tower is not cut off. Take one wide shot, then one zoomed-in shot of the sculpture and stonework as a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the sky does not turn white. When you tilt the phone up, the lines will lean inwards, so hold it as level as you can and step back rather than tilt more.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be best from the east, as the sun should be behind you and light the stone. Early or late in the day, there are usually fewer people.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship and visiting inside may be ticketed or restricted at times, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Casa Batlló is one of Antoni Gaudí's best-known buildings, and it is easy to see why it draws a camera. The façade has almost no straight lines. Instead you get rippling stonework, irregular oval windows on the ground floor and a surface of broken ceramic tiles (trencadís) that shifts from golden orange to greenish blue. Locals call it the House of Bones because of its skeletal, bony look. It stands on Passeig de Gràcia in the Eixample, in the row known as the Illa de la Discòrdia, the "Block of Discord", where four very different Modernista buildings sit side by side. That makes the street a good place to compare styles in a single walk. The house was built in 1877 and Gaudí redesigned it from 1904. The work was finished in 1906, and the building became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005. For a phone photo, the colours and curves do most of the work. Start with one wide shot of the whole building, then move in for details such as the balconies, the tile colours and the carved stone around the lower windows. Take a few shots from slightly different spots, because passers-by and street furniture can drift into the frame. If you want the whole façade without tilting the phone steeply, step back to the phone icon on the map and shoot from there.
text.geographic_location: Casa Batlló is on Passeig de Gràcia in the Eixample district, in the centre of Barcelona, at about 41.3915 N, 2.1648 E. It is part of the Illa de la Discòrdia row of Modernista buildings.

Alternatively, Provença Metro station (Metro line L6 and Metro line L7) is about 10 minutes on foot from the building, which lies to the east of that station. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade from where you stand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or a tight pavement stop you stepping back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tiles, balconies and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. This distance lets you fit most of the façade in without pointing the phone steeply upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them. Keep the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the walls lean inward. Leave a little sky above the roofline. For a detail shot, zoom in on one balcony and the tile colours around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the façade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the tile colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people on the pavement. Soft, even daylight shows the colours of the tiles best, and harsh midday sun can create strong contrast across the façade.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed from the public street, but the interior is likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: La Rambla
label: La Rambla

text.description: La Rambla is the tree-lined pedestrian street that runs for about 1.2 kilometres from Plaça de Catalunya down to the Christopher Columbus Monument at Port Vell. It sits between the old Barri Gòtic to the east and El Raval to the west. It photographs well because of the long view down the middle of the promenade: plane trees overhead, newspaper and flower kiosks, pavement cafés and a steady flow of people. It began as a seasonal stream bed. The city walls were extended to take it in from 1377, and by 1440 the stream had been diverted and the Rambla slowly turned into a street. Look down as well as up: the paving is laid to ripple like water, which is a nice nod to that past. There is also a mosaic by Joan Miró set into the promenade. The Liceu opera house is close to the phone icon on the map, so it makes a handy landmark when you line up a shot. The street is busy for much of the day and late into the evening, so plan for people in your frame. Use them as part of the scene, with movement and colour, rather than waiting for a clear gap. Keep the phone steady against your chest or a railing, and take a few frames in a row so one catches a good moment. Check the horizon and tree trunks against the gridlines so the street doesn't lean.
text.geographic_location: La Rambla is in central Barcelona, on the boundary between the Barri Gòtic and El Raval. The subject sits on the stretch near the Liceu opera house and Liceu Metro station, between Plaça de Catalunya to the north and the port to the south.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line L3 to Liceu Metro station. The subject is only 2 m from the station, to its south-west, so it is less than a minute on foot. Jaume I Metro station (Metro line L4) is 552 m from the subject, about 9 minutes on foot, with the subject to the south-west of the station. Liceu Metro station is much closer. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full canopy of trees and both rows of kiosks, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pack the crowd and the street into a tighter, more layered picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the centre of the promenade on the middle vertical line, with the tree trunks running parallel on either side. Keep the horizon level. Include a kiosk or café table in the foreground for depth, and look down for a frame that shows the wavy paving.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky between the leaves doesn't wash out. For a busy scene, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the calmest time for a clearer view. In the evening the street lamps and shop lights come on, and night mode can handle the lower light, though the crowds will be larger.

text.access_note: La Rambla is an open public pedestrian street, but it can be very crowded, especially in high season; check the official site before you go if you plan to enter any individual building along it.

name: Plaça de Catalunya
label: Plaça de Catalunya
camera_source: Commons cluster (61 photos). Moved 3 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 70 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/126299773: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Plaça de Catalunya' (101 m across).

text.description:
Plaça de Catalunya is the big open square where Barcelona's old city and the 19th-century Eixample meet. It is generally treated as the city centre. It covers roughly 50,000 square metres, so there is space to step back and fit a lot into one frame. The square was first laid out in 1902 and reworked in 1929 to designs by Francesc de Paula Nebot, which is when its metro station arrived.

It photographs well because of the layers: fountains in the foreground, statues dotted around, a compass rose set into the pavement, and city buildings on every side. The pigeons that gather in the middle add movement and a bit of everyday life. Look up at the Telefónica building too. Its tower lantern holds four stained glass windows designed in 1991 by Brian Clarke to commemorate the 1992 Olympic Games.

For a phone picture, work with the space rather than against it. Start with a wide view that shows the fountains or the pavement pattern, then move in on a single statue or a detail. Keep the phone level, using the gridlines, as the buildings around the square will lean if you tilt up. The square is busy, so wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or include people on purpose to show the scale. The phone icon on the map is a short step from Catalunya Metro station, so this is an easy stop to fit in between other sights.
text.geographic_location: Plaça de Catalunya sits in central Barcelona, on the border between the old city (Ciutat Vella) and the Eixample. La Rambla, Passeig de Gràcia and Portal de l'Àngel all start from or meet at the square.
text.directions_text: The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots, as it shows the square the way you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole space, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a single statue or the top of the Telefónica tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone level to stop the buildings leaning. Put a fountain or the pavement pattern low in the frame as a foreground, and leave some pigeons or passers-by in for scale. If you use 0.5x, keep important details away from the edges, where things can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky and pale stone keep their detail. For a statue, try portrait mode only if it's close enough to work. Otherwise a 2x-5x zoom with a tap on the figure gives a cleaner shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning for fewer people in the frame. In the evening, when the light fades, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady for sharper results.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any building or venue around it.

text.description: Casa Milà, better known as La Pedrera, is a Modernista apartment building designed by Antoni Gaudí. It was his last private residence, built between 1906 and 1912. The nickname means "the stone quarry", and it came from the rough, rippling look of the stone front, which many people in Barcelona found odd when it was new. It photographs well because almost nothing on the facade is straight. The stone seems to roll along the street, and the twisting wrought-iron balconies add dark, tangled detail against the pale surface. The stone front carries its own weight rather than hanging from a frame, which is part of why the curves could be so bold. UNESCO added it to a World Heritage listing of Gaudí's works in 1984. Take a wide view first, then move in on the balconies and the texture of the stone. Pavements near the building are likely to be busy, so be patient and shoot between passers-by. Soft, even light shows the carved surface best. Harsh midday sun can leave deep, flat shadows under the balconies.
text.geographic_location: Casa Milà stands on Passeig de Gràcia, at number 92, in Barcelona. It is a short walk from Diagonal Metro station (Metro line L3 and Metro line L5).

Alternatively, from Provença Metro station (Metro line L6 or Metro line L7) the building is about 349 m to the north-east, about 6 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the corner from where you stand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if passers-by or the pavement edge stop you stepping back. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the balconies and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From here the curved front fits in the frame without you having to tilt the phone far upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the edge of the building so the walls do not lean inward. Hold the phone level and, if you can, keep it at chest height rather than tilting up. Then take a second, tighter shot of the balconies with the zoom, leaving some empty stone around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the pale stone keeps its texture. Live Photos can help if people walk through the frame, because you can pick a cleaner moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or a bright but slightly hazy day tends to give softer light and fewer people. In the evening, night mode can help in low light if you hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public pavement, but visits inside and to the roof terrace are managed by the Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
La Boqueria is a large covered public market in Ciutat Vella, with its entrance on La Rambla close to the Liceu opera house. It is a busy, colourful place, and that suits a phone camera well. Stalls offer a wide selection of goods, including fish and meat, so you can get plenty of close-up detail pictures as well as wider views of the entrance and the crowds passing through.

The market has a long history. The first mention of a market here dates from 1217, when tables were set up near the old city gate to sell meat. The market was legally recognised in 1826, building work started on 19 March 1840, and the structure was finally inaugurated in 1853. The metal roof you see overhead today was added in 1914, so look up as well as ahead.

For photos, start at the phone icon on the map and take one wide shot towards the market. Then go in for the details: stacked produce, hanging signs and the roof structure. Keep your phone close to your body in the crowd and move slowly so you don't hold anyone up. If you want a close picture of a particular stall or the person serving, ask first. A smile and a nod usually does it.
text.geographic_location: La Boqueria is in the Ciutat Vella district of Barcelona, with its entrance on La Rambla. It stands a short walk from the Liceu opera house.
text.directions_text: The easiest start is Liceu Metro station (Metro line L3). The market is about 2 minutes on foot, roughly 130 m to the west. From Barcelona-Plaça Catalunya Metro station (Metro line L6 and Metro line L7) it is about 9 minutes on foot, roughly 528 m to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the entrance and the busy scene around it. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for stalls at a natural distance. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details across a counter without leaning in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the entrance on one of the vertical lines, with the street crowd filling the foreground. Inside, frame tight on one colourful stall, and try one shot pointing up at the metal roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stall or the face you care about to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright entrance washes out. Live Photos can catch the movement of the crowd. Hold still for a second after pressing the shutter, as the light inside can be dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, which makes it easier to take photos without crowds. Daylight outside also helps the entrance shot.

text.description:
Barceloneta Beach is a sandy beach on Barcelona's seafront, and it works well for photos because it gives you wide, open space: a long curve of shoreline, the sea and a big sky in one frame. It is also lively. On a sunny day there are swimmers, walkers and beach games to give the picture a sense of place. If you want a calmer shot, go early, when the sand is quieter and the light is softer.

The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north of the subject. From there you can capture the beach as part of the wider seafront rather than only the sand at your feet. For the full scene, use the default lens (1x) and keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines. Then switch to telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as a line of parasols, people at the water's edge or the shapes along the shore. These shots also make the distance feel shorter.

Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly. This stops the sea and sky from washing out. If you walk down to the sand, take care with your phone near water and sand, and keep a firm grip when shooting close to the waves.
text.geographic_location: Barceloneta Beach is in La Barceloneta, in the Ciutat Vella district of Barcelona, on the city's seafront.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Barceloneta Metro station (Metro line L4), with the beach to the south-east, about 11 minutes on foot. Ciutadella | Vila Olímpica Metro station (Metro line L4, with tram T5 and tram T6) is another option, with the beach to the south, about 14 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of sand, sea and sky. Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for details at a distance. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are on the sand and want a big sweep of beach, and keep the horizon away from the edges so it does not bend.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. For a closer view, walk toward the beach, about 7 minutes on foot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, not the middle. Choose a main subject, such as a line of parasols or a curve of shore, and leave some open sky or sea around it. Wait for a person or a group to walk through the frame for a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or sand to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks too bright. If you are facing the sun, hold the phone steady and take a couple of shots to be sure one is sharp. Panorama mode works for the long shoreline, if you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the sand than midday.

text.description: Parc de la Ciutadella is a large, calm park on the northeastern edge of Ciutat Vella, and it gives you plenty of different pictures in one visit: tree-lined paths, a small lake, sculpture and fountains. For decades after it was created in the mid-19th century it was the city's only green space. It covers about 31 hectares, which is why the best shots come from wandering rather than standing in one place. The ground has a heavy history. After the siege of 1714, Philip V built a huge fortress here, and much of the La Ribera district was cleared to make room for it. When the fortress was finally handed over to the city, Josep Fontserè turned the site into the park in 1872. It was then reworked for the 1888 Universal Exhibition. The big Cascada fountain is one of the park's best-known sights. It was finished in 1888, and Fontserè loosely modelled it on the Trevi Fountain in Rome. Giant crab-claw staircases lead up to its central podium, with a statue of Venus on an open shell in front. The young Antoni Gaudí may have contributed to the design. For your phone, go to the phone icon on the map and look south towards the park. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit in the sweep of paths and trees, then switch to the default lens (1x) or zoom in on sculpture and fountain details. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines. Check the park is open when you arrive, because it has been closed to the public at times.
text.geographic_location: In Ciutat Vella, Barcelona, on the northeastern edge of the old city. The park's grounds include the zoo and the Parliament of Catalonia building, and it is close to the Barceloneta and Vila Olímpica areas.

From Ciutadella | Vila Olímpica Metro station (Metro line L4, with tram T5 and tram T6 also stopping there), the park lies to the west, about 7 minutes on foot. From Barceloneta Metro station (Metro line L4) head north, about 11 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 220 m north of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use a path or tree-lined avenue as a leading line towards the centre of the picture. Keep the horizon level. For the fountain and sculpture, step back and include the steps or water in the foreground to give a sense of size.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and water don't wash out. Use portrait mode for close-ups of people or sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the paths. Midday sun can be harsh under the trees.

text.description:
Montjuïc Castle is an old military fortress on top of Montjuïc hill, with roots going back to 1640. The foundation stone was laid that year, and the fort saw its first battle in January 1641. New bastions and battlements in 1694 turned it into a castle. The structure you see today took shape in the 18th century. The old fort was demolished in 1751, and the final form came during major works between 1779 and 1799, when the castle was equipped with 120 cannons. It later served as a military museum and has been a Barcelona municipal facility since 2007. Its history is a heavy one, so a respectful tone in any captions suits it.

It photographs well because of its solid, angular walls and its position above the city. Keep the horizon level and let the walls make the strong diagonal lines. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, since walls and sky are simple shapes that look good both wide and tight. If other visitors walk through, wait a moment for a clear gap.
text.geographic_location: On Montjuïc hill, in Barcelona, about 1.3 km south of Paral·lel Metro station.
text.directions_text: Start at Paral·lel Metro station (Metro line L2 and Metro line L3). The castle is about 1.3 km to the south, which is about 21 minutes on foot. The steep hill makes the walk slower in practice. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the castle with some space around it. Then try the telephoto/zoom (2x-3x) to pick out the walls and rooflines. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and want the whole wall in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the main wall along a lower third line, with sky filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Try a second frame with a path or low wall in the foreground to add depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the castle to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone does not wash out. If the castle looks dark against bright sky, tap on the wall and raise the exposure slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely best, as the sun will be behind you and light the wall facing you. In the late afternoon you would be shooting towards the sun, so expect a darker castle.

text.access_note: The castle is a municipal facility, and parts of it may be ticketed or have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The Magic Fountain sits at the head of Avinguda Maria Cristina, below the Palau Nacional on Montjuïc, a short walk from Plaça d'Espanya. It was built for the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition, designed by Carles Buïgas, and the first show was on 19 May 1929, the day before the Exposition opened. It uses 3620 jets, and the highest spout reaches about 170 feet (roughly 52 metres). After heavy damage in the Spanish Civil War it didn't run again until 1955, and it was fully restored before the 1992 Olympics.

It photographs well because water, colour and a grand backdrop all come together in one frame. From the phone icon on the map you look along the avenue with the fountain in front and the palace rising behind it. Even when the fountain is quiet, the wide basins and the symmetry make a tidy, balanced picture. The shows, with changing coloured light and music, are what most visitors come for. They are listed as happening at half-hour intervals at weekends, with extra time in summer, so check the official site for current times before you go.

For practical advice: arrive a little early, as the best spots near the front fill up. Take a few test shots before the show starts so you know your framing, then keep your phone ready for the changing colours. Keep a hand on the screen edge to avoid smudges from spray or fingerprints.
text.geographic_location: In the Montjuïc area of Barcelona, at the foot of the hill below the Palau Nacional, at the head of Avinguda Maria Cristina (about 41.37116° N, 2.15174° E). It is close to Plaça d'Espanya and Poble Espanyol.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line L8 to Barcelona-Plaça Espanya Metro station, the nearest station. The fountain is about 462 m to the south-east, about 8 minutes on foot. Alternatively, take Metro line L1 or Metro line L3 to Espanya Metro station, where the fountain is about 471 m to the south, also about 8 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole fountain, the avenue and the palace behind. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the central jets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The fountain is straight ahead and the Palau Nacional sits behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the central jet on the middle line so the symmetry shows. Keep the horizon level and leave room above for the tallest spouts. For a different shot, try portrait orientation with the palace at the top and the water below.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the water to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the coloured lights don't wash out to white. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the jets. If you use night mode, keep your hands steady, as moving water can look smoothed or soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go for a show, which the sources say runs at weekends, and check the official site for current times. Arriving just before the show starts gives you time to find a spot and test your framing.

text.access_note: The fountain is in a public area, but show times and any restrictions can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The Bunkers del Carmel are the old anti-aircraft gun emplacements on the summit of Turó de la Rovira, a 262 m hill looking out over Barcelona. They were built during the Spanish Civil War, when the battery here had four Vickers 105 mm cannons. Afterwards the abandoned structures became shelter for families, and the shanty town of Els Canons grew up around them and lasted into the 1990s. The hill was renovated in 2011 as an outdoor heritage site, and traces of its much older Iberian settlement are part of the story too.

It photographs well because the concrete platforms are open and give a wide, uninterrupted view across the city. You get a foreground of weathered concrete, railings and people, with the districts of Barcelona spread out behind. It suits both a wide scene and a closer shot of a single landmark in the distance.

For a phone, the key is to make the concrete part of the picture instead of just pointing at the skyline. Walk around the summit before you settle on a spot, because the view changes from one platform to the next. Take a few frames of the same view at different zoom levels. Keep your phone strap or wrist loop on, and take care near edges and low walls, especially if the platforms are busy.
text.geographic_location: The spot is on the summit of Turó de la Rovira, in the El Carmel area of Barcelona. It sits on the hill above the neighbourhood and is part of the Tres Turons (Three Hills) chain, at the Turó de la Rovira end.

The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

Include a bit of the concrete or railing in the foreground to give the view depth. For a wide scan across the skyline, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour instead of turning white. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening usually works well, as the light softens and the city lights begin to come on. Check the official site for access times before planning a sunset visit.

text.description:
Palau Güell is a town mansion that Antoni Gaudí designed for the industrial tycoon Eusebi Güell. It was built between 1886 and 1888 and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for Gaudí's works. It stands on Carrer Nou de la Rambla in El Raval.

It photographs well because the entrance is full of detail. The front gates have a parabolic arch and forged ironwork that looks like seaweed, with a few parts shaped like a horsewhip. Between the two gates Gaudí placed a bronze phoenix, an emblem of the cultural and economic revival of Catalan society. Carriages once drove in through these gates, so you can picture the building as a working home rather than a museum piece.

On a phone, the street is the challenge and the details are the reward. Start with a wide shot to show how the building sits among its neighbours, then move in on the ironwork and the phoenix. Keep your phone upright for the height of the front and turn it sideways for the gate arch. If the front is in shade, tap the brightest part of the stone and lower the exposure slider a little so the metalwork stays dark and crisp. Wait a moment for passers-by to clear the frame, or let one walk through for scale.

Visits were suspended in 2004 for restoration, and the work was completed in April 2011. The interior is open to visitors, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Palau Güell is in the El Raval neighbourhood of Barcelona, on Carrer Nou de la Rambla. It sits between Liceu Metro station and Drassanes Metro station (Metro line L3).

From Liceu Metro station (Metro line L3), it is about 302 m to the south, about 5 minutes on foot. Walk to Carrer Nou de la Rambla, then go to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front into the frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view of the entrance. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the ironwork and the phoenix.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. From here you can take in the front from a little distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean. Keep the gate arch near the middle of the frame. For a close-up, zoom in on the seaweed-like ironwork and keep the phoenix on one third of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the details don't wash out. If your phone has a Live Photo or motion option, switch it on so you can pick the best frame without people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when there are fewer people around, if you can. Check how the light falls on the building when you arrive.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the street, but the interior is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Tibidabo is the hill that looks down over Barcelona, and it has views over the city and the surrounding coastline. At 512 metres, it is the tallest hill in the Serra de Collserola. The top is crowned by the Sagrat Cor church, with the Tibidabo Amusement Park beside it and the Torre de Collserola telecommunications tower a short walk away. All three can be seen from most of the city, which makes them good landmarks for your photos.

The church was designed by Enric Sagnier. Work began in 1902 and took about 60 years. A sculpture of the Sacred Heart of Jesus by Josep Miret Llopart sits on top. That gives you two kinds of picture from one spot: the church and its statue pointing up at the sky, and the wide view back across the city and along the coast.

For a phone, the view is the main prize. Take a wide shot first to show the whole city, then zoom in to pick out smaller details below. Walk a few metres along the viewing areas and the foreground changes, so look for a railing, a tree or a person to give the picture some scale. Keep your shots of the church straight by using the gridlines, and tap the sky or the stonework to set the exposure so the building does not turn too dark.
text.geographic_location: Tibidabo is the hill above Barcelona, in the Serra de Collserola, rising to the north-west of the city. The church and the amusement park sit on its summit, which has views over the city.

Vall d’Hebron | Sant Genís Metro station (Metro line L3 and Metro line L5) is close behind, with the spot about 2 km to the west of it, about 32 minutes on foot. The walk is uphill, so allow extra time, and check which services are running before you set out. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the church and want to fit the building and the statue in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Torre de Collserola, the coastline or single buildings far below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face out over the city for the view, or turn round and step back from the church to fit it in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines. For the city view, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line and use a railing or a tree at the edge as a foreground. For the church, stand back, keep your phone level so the towers do not lean, and leave some sky above the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky or the city, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and detail. If the view looks hazy, tap on a distant building to sharpen the focus and try a zoom of 2x or more.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light and warmer colours on the city. If you stay on until dusk, night mode can capture the city lights, so rest your elbows on a wall to keep the phone steady.

text.description: Casa Vicens is a colourful house in the Gràcia district and is considered Antoni Gaudí's first major project. It was built between 1883 and 1885, with the first plans drawn up a few years earlier. It is a good subject for a phone because the surfaces do the work for you: ceramic tiling, Moorish-style arches, exposed brick and small dome or temple-shaped finishes all give you pattern and colour in a single frame. Gaudí designed three facades, and the house was attached by a dividing wall to an adjoining convent. A later extension in 1925, by his protégé Joan Baptista Serra, added a new facade and left the building fully detached. The garden was once much larger but is now only a small area around the house, so you will be shooting from close range. That makes it a spot for two kinds of photo: one wider shot to show the whole house, and a few close-ups of the tilework and details. The building became a World Heritage Site in 2005. Take your time with the details, as the decoration rewards a second look. Allow a few minutes to walk around the exterior as well, because each side of the house gives a different composition. Keep your phone lens clean before you start; a quick wipe makes a real difference to sharpness on bright tiles.

text.description: The Barcelona Pavilion is a small, calm building of stone, glass and steel, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich as the German Pavilion for the 1929 International Exposition. It was taken down in 1930 and rebuilt between 1983 and 1986, using the original drawings and the footings found on the site. It is important in the history of modern architecture, and that is easy to see in a photo. Flat roof plates seem to hover over slim chrome-clad columns. Walls of marble and onyx slide past one another, and the whole building sits on a travertine base beside pools. Those pools are the main reason it photographs well. They reflect the clean horizontal lines, and the building is designed as a series of views, so almost every angle gives you a tidy composition. The small pool holds Georg Kolbe's sculpture Alba ("Dawn"), which makes a good second subject once you have your wide shot. Take a few steps either way, because the layout changes the picture quickly. Keep your phone level so the long horizontal lines stay straight, and look for reflections in the water, glass and polished stone. Inside, the walls are close together, so expect to shoot in short, tight frames rather than one big view.
text.geographic_location: The pavilion is in Barcelona, close to Barcelona-Plaça Espanya Metro station and Espanya Metro station, on the route towards the Poble Espanyol, on the grounds of the 1929 exhibition.
text.directions_text: From Barcelona-Plaça Espanya Metro station (Metro line L8) the pavilion is about 7 minutes on foot, to the south. Walk south. From Espanya Metro station (Metro line L1 and Metro line L3) the pavilion is about 9 minutes on foot, also to the south. Walk south. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall view of the roof, columns and pools. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and cannot fit the building in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the sculpture and for details such as the column reflections and stone patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and line up the roof edge and the base with the horizontal lines, so the building looks calm and level. Put the water in the lower part of the frame to catch the reflection. Then move closer and use 2x or more to frame Alba against the marble or glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright stone does not wash out. If you shoot Alba, tap on the figure itself so it stays sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in your frame, but check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: Access rules and any entry fee are not given here, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer crowds.
The pools can give clear reflections of the building when the water is still.

name: Palau de la Música Catalana
label: Palau de la Música
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/377216661: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palau de la Música Catalana' (98 m across).

text.description: The Palau de la Música Catalana is a concert hall designed by Lluís Domènech i Montaner in the Catalan modernista style. It was built between 1905 and 1908 for the choral society Orfeó Català and opened on 9 February 1908. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. The outside is a gift to a phone camera because there is so much to look at: exposed red brick, glazed tiles, mosaics and stained glass, with a big sculpture group by Miguel Blay on the corner. On the second-level balcony, two rows of columns are each covered in different multicoloured tile, mostly in flower patterns. Above them sit busts of Palestrina, Bach and Beethoven, with Wagner on the side. The street is narrow, so you cannot step back far, and the large mosaic at the very top of the front is hard to see clearly from below. That makes this a spot for details as much as for the whole building. Work in pieces: a wide shot of the corner, then closer shots of the tiled columns, the sculpture and the brickwork. If you go inside, the vestibule and staircases are richly decorated, and the foyer is more restrained but still has ceramic flowers on its brick arches. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any rules on photography.
text.geographic_location: In the Casc Antic, the old part of Barcelona, on the corner of Carrer Palau de la Música and Carrer de Sant Pere Mes Alt. It is a short walk from Urquinaona Metro station.
text.directions_text: Start at Urquinaona Metro station (Metro line L1 and Metro line L4). The Palau is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot. Follow the streets towards Carrer de Sant Pere Mes Alt and you will find the corner with the tiled columns and the large sculpture. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the corner and balcony into the frame from the narrow street. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tiled columns, the busts and the mosaic high up. If you only have the default lens (1x), take several close shots rather than one distant one.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the pavement at this corner for your wide shots, then step back along the street as far as the pavement allows for a fuller view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the columns parallel to the grid, with the phone held level, so the building does not lean. Include the corner sculpture as your main subject with the tiled balcony above it. For detail shots, fill the frame with a single column or one of the busts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the tiles and mosaics keep their colour. After dark, try night mode, and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight shows the colours of the tiles and brick best. After dark the candelabra on the columns are lit, which gives a different mood.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the street, but the interior is a concert venue and visitor site, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps in the narrow street because you cannot stand far back.
Daylight shows the tile and brick colours best.
Interior visiting arrangements and photography rules may vary and need checking on the official site.

name: Camp Nou
label: Camp Nou
camera_source: Commons cluster (46 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/34607291: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Spotify Camp Nou' (283 m across).
notes: A football stadium, but also a major visitor sight (museum and tour); state of its rebuilding not checked. Kept for the owner to decide.

text.description:
Camp Nou is FC Barcelona's home ground, and it is simply huge. It opened on 24 September 1957 and is still the biggest stadium in Spain and Europe by seating capacity. It is being renovated, with a planned capacity of 105,000. That scale is what makes it photograph well: one long, curving wall of concrete and sky, with plenty of room for people to walk through the foreground and show how big it is. The stadium was built as continuous oval stands with no open corners, so the outline looks unbroken and works well as a sweeping curve across the frame.

A few facts help when you're choosing shots. The ground opened with room for 106,146 people. It hosted the opening game of the 1982 World Cup and the football final at the 1992 Olympics. The renovation began on 1 June 2023 and is expected to finish ahead of the 2028–29 season, although the stadium reopened for competitive matches in November 2025 at reduced capacity. Expect building work to be part of the scene, so treat cranes and hoardings as part of the picture, or crop them out.

The phone icon on the map is about 130 m west of the subject. That is close for such a big building, so you will need to go wide. Take a first shot with the whole curve in, then step in for details such as crests, seats and the roofline. Keep the phone level so the stands don't lean. Check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or on a tour.
text.geographic_location: Camp Nou is in the Les Corts neighbourhood of Barcelona, at the end of Travessera de les Corts, next to the Cementiri and the Maternitat.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Pius XII (tram T1, tram T2 and tram T3), about 11 minutes on foot, with the stadium to the south. Avinguda de Xile (tram T1, tram T2 and tram T3) is also about 11 minutes on foot, with the stadium to the east. For the metro, Collblanc Metro station (Metro line L10S, Metro line L5 and Metro line L9S) is about 11 minutes on foot, with the stadium to the north-east. Palau Reial Metro station (Metro line L3, plus tram T1, tram T2 and tram T3) is also about 11 minutes on foot, with the stadium to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long curve of the stadium in from this close. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of one section. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details on the upper rim, signs and crests.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a few steps left or right to change which part of the curve sits in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon on the lower line so the stands don't tilt. Place a few people or a walking group in the foreground to show the scale. With the ultra-wide, keep the stadium away from the edges of the frame, where buildings can look stretched. Leave a wide band of sky if the cloud is interesting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stadium wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the concrete keeps its detail. Take a panorama if you want the whole length in one frame; move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The stadium's south-west-facing side is likely to be best lit in the afternoon, when the sun is behind you. Early in the day you may be shooting into the light. On match days it will be crowded, so for clean shots go on a non-match day.

text.access_note: The stadium surroundings are the place to photograph from; for tours, the museum or any interior access, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point on the map is on the south-west side of the stadium, so the stadium's south-west-facing side is likely to be lit by the afternoon sun.
Match days are busier around the stadium than non-match days.
Renovation works such as cranes or hoardings may be visible in photos.
At about 85 m, the ultra-wide (0.5x) is needed to fit a long section of the stadium into a phone frame.

name: Gothic Quarter and the Bishop's Bridge
label: Bishop's Bridge
camera_source: Commons cluster (16 photos). Moved 4 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 35 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/643140494: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The neo-Gothic bridge over Carrer del Bisbe; the district around it.

text.description:
The Bishop's Bridge (Pont del Bisbe) spans Carrer del Bisbe in the el Call area of the Gothic Quarter, the old part of Ciutat Vella. It is a good subject for a phone because the bridge arches over a narrow street, and the stone walls on either side lead the eye towards it. The result is a photo with a clear centre and plenty of depth, without any complicated setup.

Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on gridlines. Place the bridge in the middle of the frame and keep the vertical lines of the walls straight, which makes the street look tidy and calm. If you want a little more of the walls and the sky above, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps, but keep the bridge away from the very edges, where straight lines can look stretched. For a tighter, more compact view, the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) brings the bridge closer and cuts out some of the street clutter.

The lanes here can be busy with people walking through, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest foreground. Tap the bridge to focus, then lower the exposure slightly if the sky above the street looks too bright. A Live Photo can be handy for catching a moment when someone walks through the arch.

Take your time, and look up as well as along the street.
text.geographic_location: In the el Call area of the Gothic Quarter (el Gòtic) of Ciutat Vella, Barcelona, on Carrer del Bisbe.
text.directions_text: From Jaume I Metro station (Metro line L4), the bridge is 203 m to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot. From Liceu Metro station (Metro line L3), it is 350 m to the north-east, about 6 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the street and walls, or the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter view of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge in the centre of the frame, keeping the walls upright. Let the street lead the eye to the arch. Wait for a gap in the people walking through before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks too bright. Try a Live Photo to catch someone walking through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning, when the narrow street is usually quieter.

text.access_note: This is a street-level public location; check the official site before you go for any nearby buildings or visits.
claims_not_in_sources: Carrer del Bisbe is a narrow street with stone walls on both sides.
The bridge crosses over the street, so it can be photographed from street level.
The street can be busy with walkers during the day and is usually quieter early in the morning.
The sky above a narrow street can look brighter than the walls in shadow, so lowering the exposure may help.
